name: Regent hairstyle

lead: The regent is a men's haircut with sides swept back and a top left long and raised, known in Japan as riizento. It adds height and volume at the front hairline and a flowing curve at the nape, which suits people who want a dramatic, retro frame for the face.

The name first appears in British barbering manuals of the 1930s; in Japan the style arrived in Ginza in 1933, was suppressed in wartime and revived after 1947, and later became linked with rockabilly, bosozoku and yankii fashion.

paras: Barbers cut the sides long enough to sweep back and leave the top longer, then set the front with a dryer, comb and grease or pomade. Variants include permed, clippered or fringe-down versions, and the back often ends in a ducktail-like curve.

Heavy pomade and daily heat styling take time and can leave residue or dryness; the style depends on enough hair on top. In Japan it also carries a delinquent stereotype that some wearers adopt deliberately.

chain: Long top lifted and set with pomade

angle.text: The style piles volume above the forehead and sweeps the sides back, so the face reads as framed by a tall front and a clean profile. It is worn as a signature retro look.

lead: The regent is a men's hairstyle named in British barbering manuals and, as riizento, in Japan [1]. The British classification describes it as not too short, full at the sides, with the back brushed toward the centre and the top rather long [1].

In Japan the word covers hair slicked back at the sides with the top left long and raised into a pompadour, either flat and pomaded or high and loose [1]. People wear it to add forehead-line height and a retro, confident silhouette.

Accounts of the name point to London's Regent Street and to the hair of Edward VIII; a Harajuku barber told a Japanese magazine in 2016 that the curve at the nape resembles the bend of Regent Street [1].

paras: In the 1931 hairdressing manual edited by Gilbert A. Foan, the regent is a classified men's style cut short or long in the same shape, with a V-shaped nape and hair graduated upward [1]. Japanese riizento differs: sides slicked back and a top put up over the head in a pompadour [1]. A Harajuku barber says the defining part is the flowing curve at the back, a ducktail, and that versions may be permed, clippered or worn with the fringe down [1].

In Ginza, late-1920s modern boys already set an all-back look with pomade, and a regent dated to 1933 was worn by dance-hall youth and the comedian Ken'ichi Enomoto [1]. It faded in the early 1940s when pomade ran short, then returned in 1947 on black-market pomade among musicians, bartenders and teenagers [1]. Later rockabilly, bosozoku and yankii fashion lifted the front higher, and the regent came to signal youthful defiance [1][2].

In the wider pompadour history, the men's version was a 1950s fashion worn by Elvis Presley, James Dean and others, and in Japan the Regent is stereotyped with gang members, yakuza, bosozoku and yankii, with anime and manga exaggerating its size [2].
